# Mine

A set of small PWAs that keep your personal data as markdown in a private GitHub repo —
calendar, zettelkasten, diary — so it stays portable and free of vendor lock-in.

**Live: https://maximilianharr.github.io/mine/** — install it to your home screen.

## Docs

| | |
| --- | --- |
| [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) | what the app does and how it behaves |
| [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) | how it is built, and the verified platform findings |
| [TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) | what is checked before a change ships, and how |
| [calendar/](calendar/) | the calendar app, with its own pair of docs |

## Layout

```
style.css                                         the shared base: tokens and chrome
index.html app.js home.css sw.js manifest.json    the main app
shared/   apps.js store.js github.js md.js        used by every app
          markdown.js prefs.js ui.js sync.js
          vendor/
calendar/                                         one folder per app
spike/                                            on-device platform checks
test/                                             the checks: test/run.sh
```

No build step: no bundler, no CI, no dependencies to install. `git push` deploys to GitHub
Pages. To run it locally, `python3 -m http.server` in this folder and open the printed URL.
`test/run.sh` runs the model checks in node and the rest in a headless browser, and installs
nothing either.

Data lives in a **separate private repo**, never in this one. The token is entered once in the
app, stored on the device, and scoped so it can only touch that data repo.

## Status

The main app, the sync layer and the on-device checks are done and verified end to end against a
real repo. The calendar is built — the five views, the kanban, the entry popup and its field
popups, the filter and the settings — and `test/run.sh` covers it.

Not built yet: the per-app summary above the tiles that [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md)
describes. The tile screen shows tiles only, so opening the calendar is currently the only way
to see what is on today.

#!/bin/bash
# One contact sheet per theme - month, entry popup, kanban side by side under a caption - and one
# overview sheet of the eight month views.
set -eu
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
OUT=$HERE/out
SHEET=$HERE/sheets
mkdir -p "$SHEET"

names=(
  "1-graphite|1. GRAPHITE|Swiss neutral - hairline rules, one blue accent, desaturated event colours, tabular figures"
  "2-linen|2. LINEN|Warm paper - Charter headings on off-white, terracotta accent, tinted event chips"
  "3-midnight|3. MIDNIGHT|Dark first - deep navy surfaces, lifted cards, luminous tints, generous radii"
  "4-pebble|4. PEBBLE|Soft and rounded - rounded font, pill controls, big radii, indigo accent, roomier targets"
  "5-blueprint|5. BLUEPRINT|Technical and dense - visible grid, monospaced figures, square corners, outlined entries"
  "6-meridian|6. MERIDIAN|Quiet luxury - Palatino period label, forest and brass, small-caps labels, lots of air"
  "7-mono-ink|7. MONO-INK|Minimal product UI - black on white, 1px greys, layered shadows, 8% colour tints"
  "8-aurora|8. AURORA|Modern and colourful - violet primary, tinted chrome, soft gradients, confident headings"
)

for row in "${names[@]}"; do
  id=${row%%|*}; rest=${row#*|}
  title=${rest%%|*}; sub=${rest#*|}
  convert \
    \( "$OUT/$id-1-month.png"  -resize 900x -bordercolor '#c9ccd2' -border 1 \) \
    \( "$OUT/$id-2-popup.png"  -resize 900x -bordercolor '#c9ccd2' -border 1 \) \
    \( "$OUT/$id-3-kanban.png" -resize 900x -bordercolor '#c9ccd2' -border 1 \) \
    +append -background '#eef0f3' -splice 0x96 \
    -gravity northwest -fill '#11151a' -pointsize 40 -annotate +26+18 "$title" \
    -fill '#5c636d' -pointsize 24 -annotate +26+62 "$sub" \
    -bordercolor '#eef0f3' -border 18 \
    "$SHEET/$id.png"
  echo "$SHEET/$id.png"
done

# the eight month views together, two rows of four
convert \
  \( "$OUT/1-graphite-1-month.png" -resize 620x \) \( "$OUT/2-linen-1-month.png" -resize 620x \) \
  \( "$OUT/3-midnight-1-month.png" -resize 620x \) \( "$OUT/4-pebble-1-month.png" -resize 620x \) \
  \( "$OUT/5-blueprint-1-month.png" -resize 620x \) \( "$OUT/6-meridian-1-month.png" -resize 620x \) \
  \( "$OUT/7-mono-ink-1-month.png" -resize 620x \) \( "$OUT/8-aurora-1-month.png" -resize 620x \) \
  -bordercolor '#c9ccd2' -border 1 -background '#eef0f3' \
  -gravity northwest -splice 0x44 \
  miff:- | montage - -tile 4x2 -geometry +10+10 -background '#eef0f3' miff:- | \
  convert - -background '#eef0f3' -splice 0x70 -gravity northwest \
    -fill '#11151a' -pointsize 38 -annotate +22+16 \
    "Eight directions, month view:  1 Graphite   2 Linen   3 Midnight   4 Pebble   5 Blueprint   6 Meridian   7 Mono-Ink   8 Aurora" \
    "$SHEET/0-overview.png"
echo "$SHEET/0-overview.png"

content.text:
Eight directions, three shots each (month view, entry popup, kanban). Nothing in the repo was touched — no files changed, no tests run, no commits.

## The eight

| # | Name | The idea | Fonts | Entry chips | Icons |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Graphite** | Swiss neutral. Hairline rules, boxed outline nav buttons, near-monochrome chrome with one blue. | Helvetica Neue / Heros, tight tracking | Solid fill, desaturated slate / moss / plum | Outline, 1.4 |
| 2 | **Linen** | Warm paper. Off-white ground, Charter serif headings, terracotta accent. | Charter display + humanist sans body | Tinted + 2px colour rule | Outline, 1.2 |
| 3 | **Midnight** | Dark first. Navy page, lifted cells and cards, luminous tints, 15px radii. | System sans, −0.018em | Tinted on dark | Solid, 1.6 |
| 4 | **Pebble** | Soft and rounded. Rounded font, pill nav, 22px overlay radii, roomier targets. | SF Pro Rounded / Quicksand | Solid fill, friendly palette | Solid, 2.0, circular |
| 5 | **Blueprint** | Technical and dense. Real gridlines, mono figures, 2px corners, uppercase period. | Liberation Sans + mono numerals | Outlined, white, left bar | Outline, 1.3, square caps |
| 6 | **Meridian** | Quiet luxury. Palatino period label, forest + brass hairline, letterspaced caps, lots of air. | Pagella display + Cantarell | Tinted, earthy | Outline, 1.1, circular |
| 7 | **Mono-Ink** | Minimal product UI. Pure black on white, 1px greys, layered shadows, black today-pill. | Inter-class, −0.011em | 14% tint with colour as ink | Outline, 1.5 |
| 8 | **Aurora** | Modern and colourful. Violet primary, gradient topbar, colour-tinted kanban headers. | System sans, bold headings | Solid fill, saturated | Solid, 1.8, circular |

## What varies, and what I had to work around

- **Colours.** Each theme proposes its own *category* palette (work/home/health) and *stage* palette (todo/doing/done). The category colours live in your `groups.md` in the data repo, so adopting a theme means editing that file too — it is your data, not app code.
- **Fonts.** Your CSP is `default-src 'self'`, so no Google Fonts, no webfonts at all. Every stack is system fonts only. The shots render on this Linux box, so you are seeing the metric-compatible fallback (TeX Gyre Heros for Helvetica, Bitstream Charter for Charter, Pagella for Palatino, Quicksand for SF Pro Rounded); on your Mac/iPhone the first name in each stack wins and will look slightly better, not worse.
- **Icons.** Themes 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 swap the filled glyphs (trashcan, disk, house, ball, pin, person, bell, filter) for stroked outline versions — the single biggest change in how the icon row reads. The rest keep the current drawn set at a different weight and size. All of it stays inline SVG on the same 16×16 box.
- **Chip treatment** is the other big lever and is independent of the palette: solid fill (today's behaviour), tint-with-coloured-ink, or outlined-with-left-bar. Any theme can take any of the three.
- **Sizes** moved per theme: nav button size, period label 1.7–2.15rem, cell padding, entry line size, kanban card padding, overlay radii and shadows.

Two things I deliberately did **not** change, since they are behaviour rather than style: the period label format (`NOV/26`, and `2` for a sprint — spelling these out as "November 2026" and "Sprint 2" would help the professional read, say the word and I will), and the kanban's sprint-number-only header.

One caveat on the mocks: the fixture's token is intentionally invalid, so the live sync line says "token rejected". I overrode that text to a neutral in-sync line in the screenshots — the styling of that row is real, the message is not.

Unrelated: `.claude/settings.json` shows as modified in git. That is the `entire` CLI rewriting its own hook config at session start, not me; I left it alone.

Raw files: the 24 individual screenshots are in `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-max-ws-mine/249a9116-833b-48ce-a235-7c104668a764/scratchpad/skin/out/`, the theme definitions in `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-max-ws-mine/249a9116-833b-48ce-a235-7c104668a764/scratchpad/skin/themes.mjs`. Tell me which direction to take — or which parts of which (e.g. "Mono-Ink's chrome with Graphite's palette and Blueprint's density") — and I will turn it into real CSS in `calendar/style.css` and `style.css`.

# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize ones personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries,
diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be
ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in and are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you
plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.

To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case lives in a separate folder. e.g. the calendar PWA
lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each
folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look, a REQUIREMENTS.md
describing how the PWA works and a TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md describing how it is built.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how this is built, and
[TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how it is checked.

## One app, one setup

Mine installs as **one** app on the phone, with one icon. The apps in the subfolders are pages
inside it, not separate installs.

This is what makes the central requirement work: **the GitHub repo and token are entered once,
in the main app, and every app in a subfolder uses them.** Verified on iPhone and Android.

## Main app

A tile per app: its `icon.svg` above its folder name.

Above the tiles, apps may contribute a summary. The calendar's shows today's entries and the
next one — which matters, because opening the app is the only reminder that works (see below).

## First run

1. Open the app URL and add it to the home screen (iOS: Share → Add to Home Screen;
   Android: menu → Install).
2. The setup screen asks for GitHub owner, data repo, branch, and a personal access token.
3. The app tests the connection and reports clearly if it fails.

Settings are stored on the device only. The token is never displayed again after entry, and the
app warns 14 days before it expires.

Two settings belong to Mine rather than to any one app, and the same two rows appear in the main
settings and in each app's: **theme** (system, light or dark) and **date format** (auto, which
follows the device's locale, or `dd.mm.yyyy`, or `mm/dd/yy`). Both default to following the
device, so Mine looks like the rest of the phone until you say otherwise.

One convention is the same in every app: **a save icon is green and a trashcan is red**, wherever
either appears — a trashcan is red even where it only clears one field of one entry, because the
rule is the icon, not the consequence. Both are **glyphs on no
background**: a save is a green disk, a trashcan is a red trashcan. **Nothing in Mine is a filled
green button.** The weight of a primary action comes from the icon being the familiar one in the
familiar place, not from a block of colour — and a save drawn like the rest of the row cannot be
mistaken for a background that means something. The `x` that closes or abandons something is
neither green nor red, and stays plain.

A second convention follows from it: **the `x` is rightmost in every popup**, and the row ends
trashcan, save, `x`. The way out of an overlay is in the same corner wherever you are, so leaving
one is never something to look for — and that corner is worth more to the button reached for by
habit than to the one aimed at deliberately. The save keeps its familiar place beside it, which
is enough, because what makes it findable is the green disk and not the edge of the card.

## Markdown bodies

Every app keeps its text as markdown, so every app has to show it. **One renderer, in `shared/`,
used by all of them** — the calendar's details body today, a zettelkasten note and a diary entry
next. Two renderers would drift, and a note that looked right in one app and wrong in the next
would be the plainest possible sign that these files are not as portable as the whole idea claims.

It is **deliberately small**, and covers what a personal note actually holds: paragraphs, `#` to
`###` headings, bullet and numbered lists, `- [ ]` and `- [x]` checkboxes, **bold**, *italic*,
`code`, and links. No tables, no blockquotes, no fenced code blocks and no images — each of them
is more code to own for something an agenda or a diary page rarely carries, and the app that first
genuinely needs one can add it then.

A checkbox is **rendered, not operated**: `- [x]` draws a ticked box, and ticking it is an edit of
the text like any other. A body is read far more often than its checklist is advanced, and a
tappable box would have to write a file from a screen whose whole point is that it writes nothing.

**It builds nodes, never HTML.** The renderer makes DOM elements and sets text, so nothing in a
body can turn into markup: a body carrying a `<script>` tag shows that tag as text. This is the
threat the CSP exists for — injected script on our own origin — and a data file in your own repo
is the likeliest thing to carry a stray angle bracket. A link is rendered only for `http`, `https`
and `mailto`; anything else stays text, so a `javascript:` URL is never something to press. Links
open in a new tab, because leaving the app would lose the view you were in.

It is hand-written rather than vendored. It is small enough to be, and the dependency table in
[TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) asks of everything in it what would be
wrong with hand-rolling it — for this, nothing.

## Using it

- Changes appear instantly and are queued for GitHub in the background.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error. It is also a button: pressing it opens the
  calendar's `logs`, which says what the last attempt did and what is still waiting.
- Offline, the queue is kept and sent when you are back online or reopen the app. **Every open
  and every window focus retries it**, whatever went wrong last time, because a queue nothing
  retries is a queue that never empties — a browser left reporting a count it can neither
  explain nor clear.
- Editing the same entry on two devices never loses either version: the other device's version
  keeps the file, yours is kept beside it and flagged, and the sync indicator tells you there is
  something to review. Nothing is discarded and nothing is silently overwritten — but the app
  does not interrupt you to ask which to keep, because by then you are somewhere else.
- Everything works offline, including dates and search, because the app keeps a full local copy.

## Reminders

**Mine cannot notify you while it is closed.** No browser can schedule a notification for later;
this is a platform limitation, not a missing feature. Alerts are stored with each entry and
exported, and they fire while the app is open. The summary on the tile screen is the reminder.

## Updates

When a new version is deployed the app shows "Update ready — reload". It never updates while you
are in the middle of editing.

The banner appears only when the version waiting to take over genuinely differs from the one
running. A new worker can sit waiting while being identical to the active one, so "a worker is
waiting" is not the test — if it were, the banner would appear on an app with no update at all
and never go away. Reloading twice with no deploy in between must leave no banner.

## Privacy

Your data lives in a **private** repo. The app itself is public, but it contains no data, and the
token is scoped so that it can only touch the data repo.

--- Put the stages and importance in the filter, and a count on the hamburger
The group checkboxes narrowed every view; `important only` and the assignee were drawn on
the board alone and were forgotten on the next reload. So the one filter that could empty
a month was the one you could not see, and the two that could not reach a month were the
only ones it offered.

The stages and importance join the groups, in every view, applied where the groups are
applied - once, in `collect()` - and remembered per device. A stage switched off hides
tasks and nothing else, an event having no stage to be judged by; `important only` hides
whatever is not marked, events included, which is what the words say and what makes a
month of what matters. The assignee stays the board's own, a card being the one place a
name is read off an entry, so the board's `passes()` is that one test now.

The hamburger carries a small count at its top right, **one per kind of narrowing** -
groups, stages, importance, assignee - so it never passes four. One per switched-off thing
would read 16 in a repo with twenty groups and fifteen hidden, which is a true number
nobody can act on.

git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
Give Mine a look: warm paper, a serif for what is read, outlined icons

The app worked and looked like a default. White page, system sans at every size, a
cool grey palette with one blue in it, solid glyphs, and an entry drawn as a block of
its category's colour - so a month with anything in it was a wall of saturated bars and
the page behind them never showed.

Linen is the whole of Mine now, not the calendar alone. The page is a warm off-white
and the surfaces above it - a popup, a panel, a card, a tile - are a shade lighter and
edged with a hairline, which is what makes one read as lifted without a heavy border.
No colour in the set is a neutral grey. There is one accent, a terracotta, and an app
highlights its own thing with it rather than naming a colour of its own. Charter sets
what is read - a heading, the period label, an entry's title, a rendered body's
headings - and the system sans sets everything operated. The icons are outlines at a
1.2-1.4 stroke; the one deliberate solid is the stage square, which is the task marker
filled in and would otherwise be the same drawing as it.

**An entry is a tint of its category's colour with that colour as the ink**, and a rule
of it at full strength down the left edge. `views.js` hands the colour to the stylesheet
as `--c` rather than painting a background on, because the two mixes that takes are not
the same on paper as at night.

**A lit icon in the entry popup lights in its own field's colour.** The category lights
in the colour it holds, with the ball knocked out so the icon carries that category
twice over; `!` lights in the red importance is drawn in everywhere else; the rest light
in the accent. One near-black fill behind all of them said only *set*, when each of
these already has a colour that means something.

**The dark theme is the same paper at night** - a warm near-black with brown in it,
paper-coloured ink, the terracotta lifted to an amber that survives on it - and not a
second palette. Two things could not follow it while they were hexes in JavaScript: the
three stage colours, which are `var(--todo)` and friends now and resolve against
whichever theme is live, and the tint an entry is drawn with, which is a pair of
`--chip-*` mixes the stylesheet applies to the one hex the user's own data can carry.

Two checks encoded the old design and move with it: a lit category icon is now read for
the category's own colour rather than for any background at all, and the kanban's stage
colour is read off its property rather than against `#e0a500`, a hex being one theme's
answer now. `.ib` stays 2.1rem - the glyph inside it grew, the box could not, a field
row's height being fixed by it.
